name: irregular-heterogeneous-ast
intent: Implement an abstract syntax tree with more than one node type whose children live in node-specific named fields, trading a uniform children collection for self-documenting nodes and accepting node-specific traversal code.
problem: Parsed syntax does not fit one node shape: alternatives of the same grammar production carry different payloads and different children. Storing them in a single node type with a positional children collection pushes the structure into every consumer - invariants such as 'a binary expression has exactly a left and a right operand' survive only in the parser's head, traversal code indexes children[0] and children[1], and each analysis must decode the layout again.
context: Hand-written parsers, interpreters, compilers, linters and code generators - especially for small languages and DSLs - where the node set is closed and known at compile time and where node-specific operations (type computation, evaluation, pretty-printing, name resolution) matter more than generic traversal machinery. Also the natural style when the tree is built from scratch in an object-oriented language and the grammar changes rarely.
benefits: Each node's shape is declared in its own type: named, typed fields (left, right, condition, body) document the grammar production the node came from and make arity and type invariants checkable at construction.
Node-specific operations live on the node type that owns the data, so evaluation, typing and printing read the fields they need instead of decoding a generic child layout first.
Field access replaces index arithmetic: binary.left cannot silently mean the wrong child the way children[1] can when a production gains an element.

Construction from scratch is direct and readable: one constructor per grammar alternative takes exactly the children that alternative defines, which is why most programmers write trees this way by default.
Node payloads and child sets evolve independently: one node type can gain a field without forcing every other node to carry the same generic child container.
tradeoffs: There is no generic way to access a node's children, so printing, walking, counting, rewriting and serialising are written per node type and the same skeleton is duplicated across node definitions (the book shows two node types needing their own toStringTree).
Cost grows with the number of analyses, not with the tree: every new pass enumerates all node types, and every new node type or field ripples through all existing passes.
External visitors and structural pattern matching get markedly harder - which is why the sibling Normalized Heterogeneous AST keeps a uniform child list for exactly those uses.
Cross-cutting infrastructure (source positions, depth limits, hashing, rewriting) must be hand-maintained on a common base or duplicated per node type.
Heterogeneous layouts defeat uniform storage: array/arena layouts for cache-friendly batch passes are harder than with a single node shape and a child list.
Field names document invariants but do not enforce them once children are mutable; constructors and accessors have to carry that burden.

participants.responsibility: Concrete representation of one grammar-production alternative, declaring its named child fields (Binary with left and right, If with condition and body) plus the payload it owns (token, position, literal value).
Typed, named slot for exactly one child role; field type and cardinality encode the invariant the production guarantees (single child, optional child, list child).
Optional shared supertype or interface carrying cross-cutting node data (source token/span, computed type) and the minimal protocol every node honours.
Printing, evaluation, type computation or rewriting implemented per node type, reading the named fields directly instead of a generic child protocol.
Builds each node with the children the parsed grammar alternative defines, enforcing arity and field types at construction time.
Per-node walker, printer or rewriter logic that must know every node type, because there is no uniform children collection to iterate.

use_cases: Recursive-descent parsers for a small language or DSL that produce a tree consumed by a tree-walking interpreter.
Linters and analysers whose rules are attached to particular node types (a rule about if-conditions, a rule about assignments) rather than to arbitrary subtrees.
Code generators and transpilers that rebuild source from nodes and need each node's own fields to emit the right syntax and operator.
Textbook and teaching interpreters where the node set is small and the tree code should read like the grammar productions.
Compiler front ends with a stable internal IR where the grammar changes rarely and node-specific passes dominate the design.

Transpilers between two syntactically similar languages (TypeScript→JavaScript, ESNext→ES5) where each source construct maps to a specific node type with named fields holding the syntactic elements that differ between source and target.

Static analysis tools for security or code quality that attach rule implementations to specific node types (e.g., a rule that flags AssignmentExpression nodes whose right-hand side is a literal) — the named fields make the relevant code elements immediately accessible.
Educational language implementations where the AST node types map directly to the textbook grammar notation, so students can read the code and see the grammar's structure without translation.

Esprima and other ESTree-compatible JavaScript tooling, where concrete nodes such as BinaryExpression expose left/right operands and IfStatement exposes test/consequent/alternate fields to parsers, linters and refactoring passes.
Tree-sitter grammars and bindings, where field(name, rule) labels role-specific children such as an if_statement's condition and body while the parser still supports named-child and cursor traversal.
avoid_when: Generic tree walking dominates - visitors, traversal-driven analyses, structural rewriting or serialisation over arbitrary subtrees: use Normalized Heterogeneous AST with a uniform child list instead.
The node set is uniform and data-driven (JSON/XML-style documents, generic expression trees): one node shape with a child list or map is simpler than dozens of named-field types.
Many operations must be added over a closed node set: an algebraic data type with one exhaustive match per operation scales better than per-node traversal code.
A maintained AST library already parses the syntax you target (go/ast, CPython ast, Roslyn, ESTree producers): reuse its node types instead of hand-rolling a second tree.
One-pass processing suffices (interpret while parsing, streaming transform): no persistent tree is needed, so there is nothing to shape.
anti_patterns: One node type with a positional children collection that every analysis decodes by index, presented as a heterogeneous AST - the structure is uniform, so the named-field choice was never made.
Copy-pasting the traversal skeleton into every node type with no shared base or helper, so the walkers drift apart and one node silently loses a case.
Adding a node-specific method to the tree for every new analysis (evaluate, print, typecheck, optimise), turning the node hierarchy into a god hierarchy that must be recompiled for each pass.
Hand-rolling a named-field AST even though a maintained library AST exists (go/ast, CPython ast, Roslyn, ESTree), then converting between the two at every boundary.
design_principles: Correspondence to the grammar: one node type per production alternative, one field per named element of that alternative.
Make illegal states unrepresentable at the node level: the cardinality and type of each child are part of the node's declaration, not of a convention.
Cohesion: operations that need a node's data live with the node type, keeping layout and node-local behaviour together.
Separation of concerns between representation (nodes) and traversal (passes), accepting that traversal loses generic access and must be written per node.
Explicit tradeoff management: choose the irregular form while node-specific operations dominate; normalize the children when generic passes take over.
best_practices: Mirror the grammar: name node types after the nonterminal or alternative and fields after the production's elements.
Keep a common base type or interface for cross-cutting payloads - token, source span, computed type - so no node repeats them and passes can still reach them.
Validate invariants in the constructor or factory (required children present, arity correct) and make child references immutable where the language allows.
Provide exactly one shared traversal facility where the language permits it (an accept method, a walk function, generated traversal) and treat adding a node type as a checklist item for every pass.
Test with golden trees: serialise each node type canonically and compare, because a heterogeneous tree has no uniform shape to assert on generically.
When generic passes start to dominate, migrate the children representation (uniform list or a second normalized view) instead of duplicating more walkers.

Use algebraic data types (Rust enum, Swift enum, Kotlin sealed classes, TypeScript discriminated unions) where the language supports them — exhaustiveness checking at the type boundary catches a missing node type the moment it is added to the grammar.
Co-locate node definitions with the simplest operation for each node type (typically pretty-printing or equality) so the field layout stays consistent as the node evolves.
Expose a programmatic introspection API (like Python's ast.AST._fields) so tooling — linters, IDE plugins, refactoring scripts — can traverse the tree without hard-coding every node type by name.
Version the node protocol when crossing an inter-process or network boundary (e.g., language server protocol) to prevent a field rename from silently breaking consumers.
sources: Parr, Language Implementation Patterns: Create Your Own Domain-Specific and General Programming Languages (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2010) - Pattern 11, Irregular Heterogeneous AST (ch. 4, Building Abstract Syntax Trees), pp. 116-117: node-specific named child fields, no generic child access, per-node toStringTree, and the warning that heavy tree walking makes irregular children a hassle.

ESTree Spec — JavaScript AST Node Types (Kyle Fiore et al., 2014): https://github.com/estree/estree — defines concrete node classes (BinaryExpression, UnaryExpression, IfExpression) with named fields left/right/operator/argument/test/consequent/alternate, the irregular heterogeneous AST pattern in a production toolchain.

tree-sitter Fundamental Design (Max Brunsfeld, 2018): https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter — uses named fields per node type as a core design principle; grammar rules declare field names (condition:, body:, consequence:) and the runtime exposes them directly.

Aho/Lam/Sethi/Ullman, Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools 2nd ed. (Pearson, 2006): https://openlibrary.org/books/OL11815362M/Compilers — Dragon Book §2.5–2.9 on syntax-directed translation and AST construction provides the theoretical foundation for heterogeneous node design.

Cooper/Torczon, Engineering a Compiler 2nd ed. (Morgan Kaufmann, 2011): https://www.elsevier.com/books/engineering-a-compiler/cooper/978-0-12-088478-0 — Chapter 4 semantic analysis covers IR design and AST structures, discussing tradeoffs between uniform and heterogeneous node representations.

Parr's canonical Pattern 11 reference (O'Reilly): https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/language-implementation-patterns/9781680500097/f_0047.html — defines Irregular Heterogeneous AST as multiple node types with irregular named child pointers and contrasts it with a normalized child list.

ESTree ES5 AST specification: https://github.com/estree/estree/blob/master/es5.md — specifies concrete node interfaces such as IfStatement (test, consequent, alternate) and BinaryExpression (left, operator, right).

Esprima syntax-tree format documentation: https://docs.esprima.org/en/3.1/syntax-tree-format.html — documents ESTree-compatible node objects with named child fields such as BinaryExpression.left and BinaryExpression.right.
Tree-sitter Grammar DSL: https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/creating-parsers/2-the-grammar-dsl.html — field(name, rule) assigns a field name to child nodes for direct field lookup.

Tree-sitter Basic Parsing: https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/using-parsers/2-basic-parsing.html — explains named versus anonymous children and ts_node_child_by_field_name for role-specific access.

Dart SDK issue #64007: https://github.com/dart-lang/sdk/issues/64007 — documents how a single generalizing visitor chain can miss orthogonal AST capabilities and recommends explicit or unifying traversal.
